item.text: {"text":"Recent work supports combining temporal sequence modeling with item graphs. [TGCL4SR (AAAI 2024)](https://ojs.aaai.org/index.php/AAAI/article/view/28789) combines global temporal item transitions, time-interval-aware Transformers and graph contrastive learning—components compatible with training from interaction histories without pretrained language weights. [SComGNN (AAAI 2024)](https://ojs.aaai.org/index.php/AAAI/article/view/28734) emphasizes that complements can exhibit both relevance and dissimilarity, so similarity alone is insufficient. [Revisiting Graph Projections (2025)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.09209) offers a simpler alternative: infer complementary recommendations through directed, weighted projections of user–item interactions. Its query-item task differs from personalized next-item prediction; reported gains do not establish gains on this benchmark.\n\nThe closest architectural precedent, [SCG-SPRe (2021/2022)](https://doi.org/10.1145/3464302), uses separate substitute/complement graphs and candidate-dependent temporal kernels. It assumes relation graphs, which are unavailable here. A feasible adaptation hypothesis: retain SASRec, add sparse training-only transition graphs across time windows, encode titles/descriptions using TF-IDF or randomly initialized token embeddings, and learn a gate combining sequence, text-similarity and transition scores. Treat graph channels as latent associations: co-purchase does not prove complementarity, textual similarity does not prove substitution, and histories do not observe fulfilled needs or compatibility. Validate each component through ablations using the common macro validation HR@10; relation-specific suppression should remain an experimental hypothesis."}
